questions.q: What is Snowflake's three-level object hierarchy?
questions.explain: Every table lives in exactly one schema, and every schema lives in exactly one database — the same shape as database.schema.table in SQL Server.

questions.q: How does creating a database in Snowflake differ from creating one in SQL Server?
options: There is no physical file path or storage setting to configure — a Snowflake database is just a named logical container
Snowflake requires you to specify a drive letter and file size
Snowflake databases must be created through a separate desktop application
questions.explain: Unlike an .mdf file in SQL Server, a Snowflake database has no physical storage configuration — Snowflake manages the underlying storage entirely.

questions.q: What is new in a Snowflake session's context compared to a plain SQL Server connection, beyond database and schema?
options: An active role and warehouse are also part of the session context
Snowflake has no concept of a current database
Snowflake sessions cannot switch schemas without reconnecting
questions.explain: Because compute is a separate concern in Snowflake's architecture, every session also tracks an active role (who's asking) and warehouse (what's paying for compute) alongside database and schema.

questions.q: How does Snowflake handle unquoted identifiers like table names by default?
options: Case-insensitively — they are folded to uppercase internally
They are rejected unless fully lowercase
They must always be wrapped in double quotes
questions.explain: Unquoted identifiers in Snowflake are case-insensitive and folded to uppercase — orders, Orders, and ORDERS all refer to the same object unless you use quoted identifiers to force exact casing.

questions.q: Which SQL commands set the current database and schema for a session?
questions.explain: USE DATABASE and USE SCHEMA set the session's current context, which you can confirm with CURRENT_DATABASE() and CURRENT_SCHEMA().
